newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss search to yield few Holocaust funds - banker.
newsitem.headline: Swiss search to yield few Holocaust funds - banker.

text.p: A prominent Swiss Jewish banker helping probe allegations that Swiss banks are sitting on unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims said on Friday he expected hardly any money to be uncovered.
But Hans Baer, hononary chairman of Julius Baer Holding AG, said the country and its banks had to go through the audit so as to emerge with a "certificate of clean health".

Baer was named last summer to an independent panel headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker to check allegations by the World Jewish Congress and other groups that Swiss banks are still sitting on Holocaust victims' huge wealth.
Berne has curtailed banking secrecy to let the panel, which includes representatives of Jewish groups and Swiss banks, review inactive accounts opened before and during World War Two.

"From an auditing point of view, we can only hope and pray nothing will be found. My suspicion is nothing -- plus or minus -- will be found because the exercise was done in 1962 and last year," Baer told the American International Club in Geneva.
"But that is not the point. The search is to get a certificate of clean health. It has to be done," he added.

"I think if we present a certificate of clean health, we will be exonerated. People will still talk -- that you can probably never entirely avoid. I'm sure we will come through with honour," Baer said.

The panel aims to put to rest Jewish groups' suspicions about banks' credibility, reinforced when it emerged this week that Union Bank of Switzerland had mistakenly shredded some old documents from a subsidiary it acquired in 1945.

Thomas Borer, head of the government task force coordinating Switzerland's response to critics, said he was still awaiting a Zurich district attorney's report on the case, which came to light when a guard smuggled out some papers to Jewish leaders.
"I cannot judge whether this was grave, but I am taking it seriously," Borer told journalists after the luncheon.

UBS says the destruction this month of old files was a "regrettable accident" and insists no client records were lost that could assist the search for any dormant wealth of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks.
Borer also said the Swiss Federal Council, or cabinet, had not yet decided whether to contribute any federal money to a compensation fund for Holocaust victims that Jewish groups seek.

"Many Swiss feel attacked and cornered," he said. "But we must make clear the Jews are not our enemies on this issue. The Americans are not the enemies. Anti-Semitism or even anti-Americanism as we see in some papers are the wrong answer."

Baer, a prominent Zurich banker educated in the United States, rejected the idea of the Swiss government setting up a compensation fund with 40 million Swiss francs ($30 million) in 800 dormant Jewish accounts identified so far.

Instead, he called for banks to open credit lines to set up an international rehabilitation agency to finance aid projects. He dismissed as "ridiculous" suggestions that the money already found in dormant accounts be used as a goodwill gesture.
